title: ACT English — Practice Test 9
summary: A full, timed enhanced-ACT English practice test: six original essays, 50 questions in 35 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a complete practice version of the **ACT English** section, with the same length and timing as the real enhanced ACT English test: **50 questions in 35 minutes**. The scored part of the real test uses five essays (three of about 340 words with 10 questions each and two of about 185 words with 5 questions each); a sixth long essay brings the total to 50 questions, just as on test day. The essays are informational, argumentative and narrative.

items: Sit somewhere quiet with nothing else open. Put your phone away.
The timer starts when you press Start and runs for 35 minutes. Do not pause it: real timing is the whole point.

Each question shows the essay with **only that question's part** underlined and numbered. Questions about a sentence, a paragraph or the whole essay say so in the question; a number in square brackets such as [5] marks a point in the essay.
Choice A is often NO CHANGE. It is a real option: choose it when the original is already the best version.
Answer every question — there is no penalty for a wrong answer. If time is nearly up, guess on the rest.
In the real test, once time is called for a section you cannot go back to it, so practise finishing inside the time.

blocks.title: ACT English — Practice Test 9
blocks.intro: Six essays, 50 questions, 35 minutes — the same length and timing as the English section of the enhanced ACT. In the real test, only 40 of the 50 questions are scored: the others are unscored field-test questions, and you cannot tell which ones they are. In this practice test, all 50 questions count. Answer every question: there is no penalty for wrong answers. After you finish, every answer choice is explained.

questions.p:
**Passage I: Paint and Patience**

The summer I turned sixteen, my aunt signed me up for a volunteer project in her village outside Minya. The plan was __[1] simple, a group__ of teenagers would repaint the village primary school before the new school year began. I agreed mostly because my friends were going, and I imagined a week of jokes, music, and very little work.

The school stood on a quiet street near the canal. Its blue paint had faded to the colour of dust, and in some classrooms the plaster had cracked so badly that pieces fell when we touched the walls. Mr. Fathy, the retired builder who led the project, kind of inspected every room, tapping each wall with his knuckles and listening carefully. Then he handed us scrapers instead of brushes.

For three days, we did nothing but scrape. We removed old paint, filled cracks with plaster, and sanding the patches smooth. My arms ached, and my friends began to complain. "When do we actually paint?" one of them asked. Mr. Fathy only smiled. "Paint on a bad wall," he said, "is a lie that lasts one winter."

On the fourth morning, he finally opened the paint tins. Consequently, he did not let us start until he had shown us how to load a roller properly, how to keep a wet edge, and how to work from the top of a wall to the bottom. Anyone who's roller dripped had to wipe up the drops before moving on. Slowly, the classrooms changed. The walls turned a clean pale yellow, and the doors and window frames became a deep, glossy green.

On our last afternoon, a few children from the village came to see the finished school. Running her fingers along a smooth yellow wall, the paint seemed to amaze a small girl. Her mother thanked each of us, one by one, individually.

I went to Minya expecting a holiday with friends. I came home with sore arms, paint in my hair, and a new respect for work that nobody sees.
questions.q: Question 1. Which choice is best for the underlined portion? (Choose NO CHANGE if the original is best.)
questions.e: "The plan was simple" is a complete sentence, and what follows explains the plan, so a colon is right. The original uses only a comma between two complete sentences (a comma splice), and leaving out punctuation creates a run-on.
ce: The original joins two complete sentences ("The plan was simple" and "a group … would repaint") with only a comma: a comma splice.
"Which" has nothing to do in this sentence; it turns the second clause into nonsense.
Correct: the first part is a complete sentence, and the colon introduces the explanation of what the plan was.
Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation at all: a run-on (fused sentence).

questions.p:
**Passage II: The Milkmaids' Secret**

For centuries, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases in the world. It caused high fevers and painful blisters, and it killed many of the people who caught it. Survivors were often left with deep scars__[11] , some__ lost their sight.

People had long noticed that anyone who survived smallpox never caught it again. In parts of Asia and Africa, this observation led to a practice called variolation: a healthy person was deliberately given a small amount of material from a smallpox sore. Usually, the patient developed a mild case and was protected afterwards. However, the method was risky, because some patients became seriously ill. In 1721, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who had seen variolation in the Ottoman Empire, helped making it popular in Britain.

A safer method came from the English countryside. Farmers had long believed that milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild disease of cows, were protected from smallpox. Edward Jenner, a country doctor in Gloucestershire, decided to test this belief. In 1796, he took material from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes and placed it in two small cuts on the arm of James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of the man who worked for Jenner as his gardener, tending his garden. Some weeks later, Jenner exposed the boy to smallpox. Phipps did not become ill.

Jenner published his results in 1798. Many doctors were doubtful at first. In fact, within a few years the method had spread across Europe and beyond. The new treatment was named vaccination, from vacca, the Latin word for "cow."

Vaccination did not end smallpox immediately, it took nearly two more centuries of work by doctors and health workers around the world. In 1980, the World Health Organization declared that smallpox had been eradicated, the first human disease to be wiped out entirely. Today, Jenner's simple experiment is remembered as the beginning of a science that protects millions of people every year.

ce: Comma splice: two complete sentences ("Survivors were … scars" and "some lost their sight") joined by a comma alone.
Correct: a semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences.
Still a comma splice: "some of them lost their sight" is a complete sentence too.
Run-on: the two complete sentences are fused with no punctuation.

In July 1799, French soldiers were rebuilding an old fort near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, when one of them noticed a large slab of dark stone covered in writing. __[21] The stone, that is now known as the Rosetta Stone,__ turned out to be one of the most important finds in the history of archaeology.

The stone carries a decree issued in 196 BCE by a council of priests in honour of King Ptolemy V. The text itself was not especially remarkable or unusual or out of the ordinary; what mattered was the way it was written. The same message appears three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic, and in ancient Greek. Because scholars could still read Greek, the stone offered a key to the two Egyptian scripts, which no one had been able to read for many centuries.

Even with this key, the work was slow. Several scholars, including the English scientist Thomas Young, made progress on the puzzle. The final breakthrough came from the French scholar Jean-François Champollion, who in 1822 announced, that he could read the hieroglyphs. Since 1802, the stone has been displayed in the British Museum in London.

**Passage V: Trains Under the City**

By the middle of the nineteenth century, London's streets were so crowded with carts, carriages, and people on foot that crossing the city could take hours. __[36] One solution seemed almost impossible: to build a railway underground.__

On 10 January 1863, the Metropolitan Railway opened between Paddington and Farringdon. It was the first underground railway in the world. Its trains were pulled by steam engines, so the tunnels were often kind of smoky. Even so, passengers crowded onto the trains from the very first day, glad to travel beneath the traffic instead of through it.

The early lines were built using a method called "cut and cover." Workers dug a deep trench along a street, built the tunnel inside it, and then covering it again. This method caused great disruption to the streets above. Later, engineers learned to dig much deeper tunnels, and in 1890 the first deep electric line opened, with trains that produced no smoke at all.

Today, the London Underground, known to Londoners as the Tube carries millions of passengers every day, and cities around the world have built underground railways of their own.

**Passage V: Trains Under the City**

By the middle of the nineteenth century, London's streets were so crowded with carts, carriages, and people on foot that crossing the city could take hours. One solution seemed almost impossible: to build a railway underground.

On 10 January 1863, the Metropolitan Railway opened between Paddington and Farringdon. It was the first underground railway in the world. Its trains were pulled by steam engines, so the tunnels were often kind of smoky. Even so, passengers crowded onto the trains from the very first day, glad to travel beneath the traffic instead of through it.

The early lines were built using a method called "cut and cover." Workers dug a deep trench along a street, built the tunnel inside it, and then covering it again. This method caused great disruption to the streets above. Later, engineers learned to dig much deeper tunnels, and in 1890 the first deep electric line opened, with trains that produced no smoke at all.

Today, the London Underground, known to Londoners as __[40] the Tube carries__ millions of passengers every day, and cities around the world have built underground railways of their own.

ce: The extra information opens with a comma after "Underground" but never closes, so it runs into the verb.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences, and it splits the subject from its verb.
Correct: the second comma closes the pair around "known to Londoners as the Tube".
A colon cannot come between a subject and its verb.

questions.p:
**Passage VI: What the Sieve Taught Me**

Last winter, I spent two weeks as a volunteer with a team of archaeologists who were excavating the remains of an ancient village near Aswan. I had seen documentaries about famous discoveries__[41] , so I expected__ to spend my days uncovering golden treasures. On my first morning, the team leader, Dr. Samira, handed me a wooden frame with a wire mesh stretched across their bottom.

"This is a sieve," she said. "Every bucket of soil from the trench goes through it. Your job is to find anything the diggers missed."

I nodded politely, but inside I was disappointed. Sieving soil did not sound like the work of an explorer.

For the first few hours, I found nothing but pebbles. I shook the sieve, picked through the stones, and tipped the leftovers onto a growing pile. The sun climbed higher, and my enthusiasm began to disappear and fade away.

Then, just before lunch, something small and orange caught my eye. A tiny piece of pottery, no bigger than my thumbnail, with a thin black line painted along one edge. I almost threw it away. Instead, I carried it to Dr. Samira, who turned it over in her fingers for a long time. I held my breath.

"This is exactly what we need," she said. The black line, she explained, was typical to the decoration of one particular period. Because of this, the fragment helped the team to date the layer of soil it came from. A golden treasure might have been more exciting to look at, but it would not necessarily have told the team more.

For the rest of my two weeks, I sieved more carefully and with greater care than ever before. I found a few beads, a bone needle, and a great many more pebbles. I never uncovered a single golden object, and I no longer wanted to. I had learned that in archaeology, the smallest pieces often tell the biggest stories.
questions.q: Question 41. Which choice is best for the underlined portion? (Choose NO CHANGE if the original is best.)
questions.e: The documentaries led the narrator to expect treasure, a cause and an effect, so "so" is right. "But" and "although" wrongly suggest the two ideas conflict.
ce: Correct: watching documentaries about famous discoveries is the cause of the narrator's expectation, so "so" shows the right relationship.
"But" signals a contrast, yet the expectation follows naturally from the documentaries.
"Although" also signals a contrast that does not exist.
"Unless" sets up a condition, which makes no sense here.
